newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton-Jiang accord grabs spotlight at APEC forum.
newsitem.headline: Clinton-Jiang accord grabs spotlight at APEC forum.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin broke the ice on U.S.-China relations on Sunday, and gave a lift to Asian and Pacific leaders gathered in the Philippines for a trade summit.
On the eve of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, the presidents agreed to exchanges that will take Jiang to Washington in 1997 and Clinton to Beijing the following year.
The summits would end a high-level frostiness lasting for almost a decade since the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.

The news grabbed centre stage from a protest by thousands of leftwing demonstrators who piled into jeepneys -- gaily-decorated minibuses styled after World War Two American army jeeps -- and headed for the summit site in Subic Bay north of Manila.

But while Clinton and Jiang emerged smiling from their 85-minute meeting, the United States and China remained at odds over Chinese membership of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which sets the rules for global commerce.
Clinton told Jiang that Beijing had to do more to open its markets.

In a separate meeting on the fringes of the APEC summit, intended to chart a course for the world's largest free trade zone around the Pacific, Clinton told Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto their countries must settle trade disputes over insurance and aviation.
He highlighted the row over deregulation of Japan's insurance market as the most important two-way trading problem, according to a Japanese official.

During a session with South Korean head of state Kim Young-sam, Clinton and Kim called on Pyongyang to take unspecified "acceptable steps" to cool tensions following the incursion of a North Korean submarine to the South in September.

Philippine authorities have warned of possible terrorist attacks during the summit in Subic Bay, and on Sunday thousands of leftist demonstrators in three motorcades of about 500 vehicles headed for the former U.S. naval base north of Manila.
Trailing banners reading "Junk APEC" -- and some of them carrying Roman Catholic nuns saying rosary prayers -- the jeepneys were stalled by a series of police roadblocks.
"We are anti-APEC because we believe APEC is no good for poor people. It can't do any good for us," said 24-year-old factory worker Eddie Mission.
Opponents say developing countries will be overrun by transnational corporations from rich nations if they open their economies, and free markets will create mass unemployment.

APEC has set a deadline of 2010 for developed members to completely open their economies and 2020 for developing countries. It envisages a borderless economy embracing two billion people with more than half of global economic output.
Asia-Pacific businessmen emerged from a two-day meeting running parellel to the APEC meeting with a rich haul -- business deals worth over $2 billion and contacts to bring more business.
At least 20 agreements were finalised between U.S. and Philippine companies, said Rizalino Navarro, former Philippine trade and industry secretary.

Meanwhile, the United States was still pressing APEC to give unequivacal backing to its plan to abolish tariffs on information technology by 2000. On Saturday ministers simply urged the WTO to reach agreement on the plan at its first ministerial meeting in Singapore next month.
APEC officials indicated that Clinton would raise the issue during Monday's summit.

Clinton's visit to Beijing would be the first by a U.S. president since George Bush there in 1989, shortly before Chinese troops and tanks killed hundreds of student democracy activists and sent relations into free-fall.
Hashimoto welcomed the announcement. "I am very happy the U.S.-China summit was conducted in a good atmosphere," a senior Japanese official quoted him as telling Clinton.
"It is not advisable to seek the isolation of China, and China is our important partner in this region," Hashimoto said.
